HoRRID MURDERS AND MUTILATIoN IN ALGERIA.-A
frightful crime was last week committed near Setif
department of Constantine, in Algeria. 4 man
named ellison, manager of large farm belonging
to the deputy mayor of Setif at about three miles
from the town, had Just terminated supping with
his wife two daughters, and an old aunt, when the
trampling of horses feet heard at the gate Of
the court yard. The old woman went to open the
cate and at the moment she did so an Arab tried to
plunge dagger into her breast but she raised her
hand, and the weapon went through it. Hearing
her cries Gibson went out and saw several Arabs,
two of them on horseback. He was Immediately
seized by them, dragged some little distance, and
stabbed repeatedly, until he fell bathed in blood,
and apparently dead. Having, however, endeavor-
ed to raise himself the Arabs seized him anew and
drew a sword across his throat, nearly severing his
head from his body. After this they went towards
the house, but Madame Gibson and her eldest daugn
ter aged It, closed the door, and pressed against 1t
to prevent them from entering. The Arabs, how
ever, forced it open and then stabbed Madame
ellison, until she was dead they next attacked the
unfortunate daughter, and cut open her skull,
plucked out eye greatly injured the other, and
cut off both her hands at the wrists. After tins
they entered the house, and ransacked the drawers
and closets, taking away everything of value. Gil
sons Youngest daughter, who had accompanied her
father when he went out, slipped away unperceived
by the assassins, and reached neighboring farm !;
the old aunt also escaped to another farm and the
occupants of these FARMS on hearing this dreadful
tale hurried towards Gilson's house. They met
the Arabs leaving it, and the assassns attacked
them with swords, driving them all away, and
woundng some The Arabs then retired. The
next day the French local authorities searched all
the houses and tents of the Arabs in the neighbor-
hood, and arrested not fewer than fourteen. One
of them was recognised by the aunt as the one who
stabbed her; another by the girl, who though so
horribly injured, is not dead, as one OF those who
assailed her.

Kansas Journal of Commerce., writing from Santa

Major Wells, connected with the stage line. ar
rived here this morning from on the Neosho mail
route, having deemed it unsafe to proceed with the
mail, after hearing of the deplorabe disaster
which, he informs me, occurred to the last outgo-

Albuquerque on the 18th instant, for NeoSho, had
some of their animals stolen by the Indians, the
Camanches, of the Plains, which the party, how
ever, pursued and recovered. The Indians there
upon largely reinforced themselves and attacked
the mail party, which after several repulses they
eventually succeeded in overpowering. The entire
party was massacred, and all the outfit including
the mail, was destroyed.


Maj. Wells learned these facts from some Pueblo
Indians, who came into the settlements and report
ed the facts. These Indians brought with them as
evidence of their statements, of the spokes of
the stage wheels and some of the curtains of the
carriages. Their story is fully credited here espe
cially by those who know that the mail party CON
sisted of but five six men, and that the Indians
on the route had declared vengeance against any
party that might attempt to open a new road
through their country.


The Pueblos state that the mail men fought long
and well before they were overcome by the greatly
superior numbers of their red enemy,

MILE RACE FOR PURSE OF TWO THOUSAND


DOLLARS BETWEEN LIZZIE MCDONALD AND


TAR RIvER-THE HORSE THE WINNER IN TWO


STRAIGHT HEATS-TIME SEVEN FORTY THREE,

The present meeting at this course closed yester-
day with the best race ever witnessed upon the
track, and one that will successfully vie with any
of its kind ever run in this section while the
cords of racing in this country do not show in
stance where horses were better matched, in point
of both endurance and speed. There four

las |, and Slasher-the two latter paying forfeit,

covered from ameneSs produced by his late contest
with the two former over the Fashion course.

while the track in fine condition, and the at
tendance somewhat increased over previous days,
though limited for race of this character Pre-
vious to the start the betting was spirited though
even the hackers of the mare being largely in the
ascendancy. In fact, the money staked upon the
horse was principally by one party, gentleman of
New York-he having, when the horses were
brought to the score, made number of bets in
which he gave odds of 500 to S75 on the horse
They both appeared in the best possible condition,
evincing an eagerness to get off which gave pro-
mise of sharp work. The horse carried one hun
dred and ten pounds, and the mare one hundred and
seven, she having won the track


First Heat.-Upon the first trial they got off well
together, and ran neck and neck to the quarter
post, both being under hard pull. In the same





seconds. From this to the head of the home stretch
there was but little variation, each laying back for
''brush'' down to the stand, and before reaching
it the mare had opened gap of one length, which

side and side. They did not, however, long con-

one length before reaching the stand, which he led

post upon the third mile, but in going up the
back stretch the again up with
the horse and they entered the home stretch

down to the stand, which the horse passed half

horses were put to their best speed, ran the first
three quarters thereof without the variation Of
length, again entering the hCme stretch neck and
neck. Here contest of the most exciting descrip
ton down to the stand for this heat took place, but
the horse showed an advantage in point of speed of
half length in the quarter, thus wining the heat

This result had the effect of rendering the horse
the favorite at heavy odds, the betting being at
three, and four to one. on him. Neither horse

quarter post when the mare closed with him in
going up the back stretch but the sneed he had in

he leading her home that distance in 1571% The
horse held this advantage until the quarter post

Will at heart to win; but the speed of the horse

Marrow ESCAPE OF RAILROAD TRAIN.-The ex-
press train on the Hudson River Railroad on Friday
morning had narrow escape, as briefly mentioned
by telegraph The train rounding curve.
about five miles beyond Peekskill, when the engi-
neer saw rock upon the track, weighing two or
three hundred pounds short distance ahead. The
signal was given for the stoppage of the train, and
the engineer seized the rope which communicates
with the patent brakes. The effect was magical;
the train was running before the brakes were an
piled, forty miles hour and the reaction was such
that passengers were almost thrown from their seats


The wheels grated along the track, and from the
time when the brakes were applied to the stopping
OF the train, it had not gone hundred yards. The
rock was fortunately severed in two, and no serious
injury was sustained. The place where the rock
road. The river is not less than eleven hundred
feet deep just beyond the rocks where the train was
liable to have been thrown, and the curve in the
road served to conceal all appearance of danger.
until too late to avoid it. Had the rock not parted
when struck, or had the brakes been of the ordi-
nary Kind, the worst consequences must have re-
suited. -

ST.. LOUIS April l4.-Frightful consequences are
likely to ensue along the lower Mississippi, which
is now higher in some places than ever known be-
fore, by the accession of the combined floods from
the upper rivers running into the Mississippi which
are rising from st. Paul down. The Missouri and
Illinois rivers both high and rising and all their
tributaries at food height. The high water is
occasioned by the heavy rains which have extended
through the whole western and northwestern com-
try. The usual spring mountain rise has not yet
taken place, and should it do before the present
flood subsidies, the whole lower country, doubtless
will be inundated.
